description_full: Kulicke and Soffa Industries, Inc. designs, develops, manufactures, and sells capital equipment and consumables in China, the United States, Taiwan, Malaysia, Japan, the Philippines, Korea, Hong Kong, and internationally. It operates through four segments: Ball Bonding Equipment, Wedge Bonding Equipment, Advanced Solutions, and Aftermarket Products and Services (APS). The company provides services used to assemble semiconductor devices, such as integrated circuits, power discretes, light-emitting diode (LEDs), and sensors. It also offers ball bonding equipment, wafer level bonding equipment, and wedge-related bonding equipment; and advanced display, die-attach, and thermocompression systems and solutions, as well as tools, spares, and services for equipment. In addition, the company services, maintains, repairs, and upgrades equipment; and sells consumable aftermarket solutions and services. It serves integrated device manufacturers, outsourced wedge and wedge semiconductor assembly and test providers, other electronics manufacturers, foundry service providers, and automotive electronics suppliers primarily in the United States and the Asia/Pacific region. The company was founded in 1951 and is headquartered in Singapore.

financial_summary: Kulicke and Soffa Industries, I is a mid-cap technology business with a $2.9B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 47%.

The business throws off $50M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.39×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.9%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 3.6% of the shares.

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 11pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 109% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 27% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 60% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $46.49 (margin of safety -18%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 39%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $28.53 to $78.82 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Technology peers: cheaper on P/E 16.0 vs 24.4 and EV/EBITDA 12.0 vs 16.1, richer on P/FCF 57.1 vs 23.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 22% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $77.00 on average, 41% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 12.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.15).
It runs a 47% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.39x.
ROE of 19% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 7pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 14.6% of revenue on R&D and 2.3% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $478.5M.
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation.
Working capital ties up about 196 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.8% over 3 years, -4.9% over 5 years and 6.6% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 46%).
At current returns, reinvesting 92% of profits supports about 6.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -29.0% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 1.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is -3, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 19.2% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.6%, and institutions hold 94%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.9% (0.4% in buybacks and 1.5% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 2,500 employees, each generates about $473K of revenue, 1.2x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 2.4% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $20K of free cash flow per employee.
Compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
